_comment: Asset-agnostic interior equipment contract (Interior Kit board). Replace asset_scene paths when final models are delivered; game effects and room rules stay stable. footprint is in 1.5 m half-cells; height is the greybox height in metres. status: catalogue = has game effects, future = modelled now with game logic later, cosmetic = no resource effect. mount_height lifts wall/ceiling items off the floor; walkthrough items have no collision.

equipment.label: Crew Bunk
equipment.description: Personal berth with reading lamp, privacy curtain and shelf.
equipment.role: One berth; lamp off on grid failure
equipment.system_note: Crew need about eight hours of sleep every sol. Each bunk gives one person a bed, so a habitat needs a bunk for every crew member. The reading light runs on the habitat's electricity: switch it off when you're done, because at night the solar panels make nothing. The curtain gives privacy, which matters on a mission that lasts years.

equipment.label: Personal Locker
equipment.description: Personal supplies and EVA storage.
equipment.system_note: Every astronaut brings clothes, tools and a few personal things, and floor space in a habitat is precious. Lockers keep belongings stowed, so rooms stay safe and uncluttered and nothing floats loose in an emergency.

equipment.label: Common Table
equipment.description: Shared meal and planning surface with inset display.
equipment.system_note: Eating and planning together keeps a small crew working as a team. The table's console shows the habitat's live status: the same readiness checks Mission Control uses to plan the next sol.

equipment.label: Task Light
equipment.description: Adjustable wall-mounted work light.
equipment.system_note: A small light aimed at your work uses far less power than lighting a whole room. On Mars every watt counts, especially at night when the solar panels make nothing, so switch it off when you leave.

equipment.label: Privacy Divider
equipment.description: Folding three-panel screen.
equipment.system_note: Living for months in a small space with the same few people is stressful. Dividers make a private corner without the cargo mass of building another room.

equipment.label: Exercise Station
equipment.description: Compact resistance trainer with display.
equipment.system_note: Mars gravity is only 38% of Earth's, so bones and muscles slowly weaken. Astronauts exercise about two hours a day to stay strong enough to work, and fit for the return to Earth.

equipment.label: Science Workbench
equipment.description: Analytical workstation with screen, sample tray and tool rail.
equipment.system_note: The crew's main bench for studying what rovers and spacewalks bring back. Drilled cores show layers of rock and dust laid down over millions of years, and the sealed chamber tests buried ice. Clues like these help scientists work out how Mars's surface has changed, and whether it once had liquid water.

equipment.label: Microscope Station
equipment.description: Close-analysis bench with image monitor.
equipment.system_note: Up close, the shape and texture of tiny grains tell a story: wind-polished, water-cemented or fresh from a volcano. Studying grains helps explain how Mars's rocks formed and changed.

equipment.label: Sample Storage Cabinet
equipment.description: Tagged sealed sample archive.
equipment.system_note: A cold, dry archive for ice, cores and rock samples. Careful storage keeps samples unchanged so they can be compared, tested again later, or one day sent back to Earth.

equipment.label: Grow Tray
equipment.description: Vertical-slice hero: lit crop rack, reservoir and nutrient line.
equipment.system_note: Plants turn light, water, nutrients and carbon dioxide into food and oxygen. Three tiers of crops under LED grow lights fit a lot of growing into a small floor space. If the lights go off, the plants stop growing, so the food supply depends on the power supply.

equipment.label: Seedling Station
equipment.description: Germination bench with humidity dome.
equipment.system_note: Young plants are fragile, so they start here under a clear lid that keeps them warm and humid. Once they're strong enough they move to the grow racks, so new crops are always coming through to replace the ones you harvest.

equipment.label: Nutrient Mixer
equipment.description: Dosing tanks and plumbing manifold.
equipment.system_note: On Mars there's no rich soil, so plants grow in water with dissolved nutrients (hydroponics). This mixer measures and doses those nutrients into the water that feeds every grow tray. The wrong mix stunts or kills the crops.

equipment.label: Harvest Cart
equipment.description: Movable crop collection cart.
equipment.system_note: Moves harvested food to the galley and stores. Inedible stems and leaves go to waste management to be recycled, so the habitat's nutrients go round in a loop rather than being thrown away.

equipment.label: Large Planter
equipment.description: A deep, shielded planter for larger crops, grown indoors under LED lighting.
equipment.system_note: A deep, well-shielded planter for bigger crops such as potatoes and tomatoes. It grows indoors under grow lights, because a glass greenhouse would expose the crops and crew to Mars's dangerous radiation.

equipment.label: Air Recycler
equipment.description: CO2 scrubber cabinet with fan, filter cartridges and ducts.
equipment.system_note: Every breath the crew takes uses oxygen and adds carbon dioxide. The recycler pulls air through filters that scrub out carbon dioxide and dust, and pumps fresh air back into the habitat. Without it, the air becomes dangerous within hours. Switch it off and watch what happens to the habitat's air.

equipment.label: Water Reclaimer
equipment.description: Grey-water recovery and filtration columns.
equipment.system_note: Water is too heavy to ship from Earth, so almost all of it is recycled: wash water, condensation from the air and even urine are filtered and cleaned to drinking quality. About 90% of the water gets reused again and again.

equipment.label: Oxygen Reserve
equipment.description: Emergency oxygen bank with gauges.
equipment.role: Stored oxygen — never created from nothing
equipment.system_note: Backup oxygen stored under pressure. If the air recycler fails, or someone uses the airlock, these tanks keep the crew safe while repairs are made. The valves and regulator control how fast oxygen flows into the habitat.

equipment.label: Thermal Control Unit
equipment.description: Heat exchanger, pump and hot/cold loops.
equipment.system_note: Mars nights drop to −80 °C, while people and machines make heat inside. This unit pumps coolant through hot and cold loops, moving heat to where it's needed and dumping the rest outside, so the habitat stays at a comfortable temperature.

equipment.label: Cargo Rack
equipment.description: Secured shelving with strapped bins.
equipment.system_note: Holds supplies delivered from Earth, secured so nothing shifts during landing or dust storms. Everything here counted against the mission's cargo budget.

equipment.label: Tool Bench
equipment.description: Repair and EVA prep bench with pegboard and vice.
equipment.role: Three working drawers; future maintenance efficiency
equipment.system_note: With Earth months away, the crew has to fix things themselves. The tool bench, vise and spare parts let them repair anything from a fan to a suit part.

equipment.label: GAR-Y Dock
equipment.description: GAR-Y's charging dock: a pad it reverses onto and a pylon whose plug slides into its rear bumper.
equipment.system_note: Rovers let the crew travel kilometres to collect samples and check equipment. They run on batteries recharged from the habitat's power grid, so long drives are planned around the power the habitat can spare.

equipment.label: EVA Tool Station
equipment.description: Rover and EVA service bench.
equipment.system_note: Where the crew prepares for work outside: tethered tools, sample bags and dust brushes. Good preparation keeps EVAs short and safe.

equipment.label: Suit Rack
equipment.description: Pressure suit storage and drying rack.
equipment.system_note: Pressure suits are personal spacecraft: they supply oxygen, keep the right pressure, control temperature and protect against dust and radiation. They're checked and serviced here between every EVA (spacewalk).

equipment.label: Corridor Light Strip
equipment.description: Low-profile route lighting at the wall base.

equipment.label: Wayfinding Panel
equipment.description: Room directions and emergency route.

equipment.label: Fire Safety Station
equipment.description: Extinguisher, fire blanket and first-aid drawer in one safety point.
equipment.system_note: Fire is one of the most serious dangers in a sealed habitat. Each safety station holds an extinguisher, a fire blanket and first-aid supplies, ready for the first person on the scene.

equipment.label: Utility Conduit
equipment.description: Pipe and cable run with brackets.

equipment.label: Airlock Control Panel
equipment.description: Cycle and pressure status display.

equipment.label: Suit Service Panel
equipment.description: Suit oxygen and power umbilicals.

equipment.label: Dust Grate
equipment.description: Regolith capture flooring.

equipment.label: Emergency Supply Locker
equipment.description: Emergency oxygen bottles, survival kits and thermal packs.
equipment.system_note: Backup oxygen, survival kits and thermal packs, kept ready in case a system fails. Good habitats have emergency supplies in more than one place.

equipment.label: Power Distribution Cabinet
equipment.description: Breaker cabinet, door open.
equipment.system_note: Every watt from the solar panels and reactor passes through here before it reaches the rooms. Breakers protect each circuit, and the big orange main isolator can cut the whole habitat off from its power, which engineers do before working on the wiring. Try switching it off and watch what loses power.

equipment.label: Battery Bank
equipment.description: Stacked storage modules with charge bars.
equipment.system_note: Solar panels only work in daylight, but the crew needs power all night too. Batteries store spare daytime electricity so the air recycler, heaters and lights keep running after sunset. The more batteries you have, the longer you can last on stored power.

equipment.label: Galley Counter
equipment.description: Primary food-preparation counter for packaged meals and ingredients.
equipment.system_note: The habitat's kitchen: a food warmer, sink and storage. Cooking is mostly reheating, but preparing food together is part of crew life.

equipment.label: Pantry Cabinet
equipment.description: Dry-food storage cabinet with labelled meal bins.
equipment.system_note: Long-life food shipped from Earth, stored until the hydroponics bay grows enough fresh food to supplement it.

equipment.label: Water Dispenser
equipment.description: A refill point for crew drinking water.
equipment.system_note: Clean drinking water from the Water Reclaimer. Watching this tap is a good reminder that the habitat's water goes round in a loop.

equipment.label: Low-Water Wash Station
equipment.description: A basin, metered tap and hand sprayer that use as little water as possible.
equipment.system_note: Washing keeps the crew healthy, but water is precious. This station uses short metered bursts and sends the used water back to be recycled.

equipment.label: Vacuum Toilet
equipment.description: Compact vacuum toilet with a sealed waste connection.
equipment.system_note: A spacecraft-style toilet that uses air flow instead of water. Waste is collected, and urine is recycled into clean water by Life Support, so even the bathroom is part of the water loop.

equipment.label: Medical Supply Cabinet
equipment.description: Lockable cabinet for medicines, trauma kits and diagnostic supplies.
equipment.system_note: Medicines, bandages and diagnostic kits brought from Earth. With no pharmacy for millions of kilometres, supplies are planned for every likely problem, and used carefully.

equipment.label: Medical Exam Cot
equipment.description: A compact examination and recovery cot.
equipment.system_note: The crew's doctor uses the exam cot for check-ups and treatment. Space travel affects bones, muscles, eyes and mood, so regular checks catch problems early, far from any hospital.

equipment.label: Waste Sorting Unit
equipment.description: Three colour-coded chutes over a compactor: sort, squash and seal waste.

equipment.label: Communications Data Rack
equipment.description: Radio and data equipment that keeps the habitat in touch with Earth and the rovers.
equipment.system_note: Radio and data equipment that links the habitat to Earth, orbiting satellites and the rovers. Messages take minutes to cross between planets, so the crew must solve most problems themselves.

equipment.label: Mess Booth
equipment.description: A curved six-seat booth around a shared table, with backless benches set back for easy getting in and out.
equipment.system_note: A shared table where the whole crew can sit together. Eating and talking together matters for wellbeing on a long, isolated mission.

equipment.description: A portable kit for cuts, burns and sprains. Place it on a floor or a table.
equipment.label: First Aid Kit
equipment.system_note: For everyday cuts, burns and sprains. Small injuries are the most common medical problem on a mission, so kits are kept close to where people work.

equipment.description: The same first aid kit on a wall bracket, at chest height where anyone can find it.
equipment.label: Wall First Aid Kit
equipment.system_note: For everyday cuts, burns and sprains. Small injuries are the most common medical problem on a mission, so kits are kept close to where people work.

equipment.description: A battery work light for repairs in dim corners.
equipment.label: Portable Work Light
equipment.system_note: A battery light for repairs in corners the ceiling lights don't reach. It runs on its own battery, so it still works during a power cut.

equipment.description: A sealed small crate of spare supplies.
equipment.label: Supply Crate (Small)
equipment.system_note: A sealed crate of spare supplies delivered from Earth.

equipment.description: A sealed medium crate of spare supplies.
equipment.label: Supply Crate (Medium)
equipment.system_note: A sealed crate of spare supplies delivered from Earth.

equipment.description: A sealed large crate of spare supplies.
equipment.label: Supply Crate (Large)
equipment.system_note: A sealed crate of spare supplies delivered from Earth.

equipment.description: The desk where the crew plans each day's work and checks the habitat's systems.
equipment.label: Mission Planning Console
equipment.system_note: The crew plans each day here: who works on what, what needs fixing, and which places to explore. Its lamps show the habitat's readiness at a glance.

equipment.description: A live map of the landing site and a globe showing where on Mars the habitat stands.
equipment.label: Mars Survey Board
equipment.system_note: A live map of the landing site from the habitat's own data, showing your rooms, buried ice, the rover and you. Switch to the globe to see where on Mars the habitat stands.

equipment.label: Wall Cabin Heater
equipment.description: A wall-mounted heating panel with Off, Low and High settings.
equipment.system_note: A backup heater for one room. It turns electricity into warmth: the higher the setting, the more power it uses. It only works while the habitat has power, and Life Support's climate control is still the main heating.

equipment.label: Portable Utility Heater
equipment.description: A movable fan heater with Off, Low and High settings.
equipment.system_note: A fan heater that can be moved wherever it's needed, such as a cold workshop or a room whose climate control has failed. It warms faster than the wall heater, but uses more power.

equipment.label: Small Cargo Crate
equipment.description: A small sealed case for supplies delivered to the surface.
equipment.system_note: Every kilogram landed on Mars costs fuel, so supplies arrive packed tightly in tough, sealed crates.

equipment.label: Large Cargo Crate
equipment.description: A large sealed case for supplies delivered to the surface.
equipment.system_note: Every kilogram landed on Mars costs fuel, so supplies arrive packed tightly in tough, sealed crates.

equipment.label: Loaded Cargo Pallet
equipment.description: A pallet of strapped-down cargo cases.
equipment.system_note: Deliveries land on pallets with everything strapped down for the bumpy descent. The crew unload them and move the supplies inside.

equipment.label: Communications Mast
equipment.description: A tripod mast with a dish and antennas.
equipment.system_note: A tall mast sends signals further: up to satellites orbiting Mars and out to rovers working beyond the horizon.

equipment.label: Outdoor Workbench
equipment.description: A sheltered bench for repairs outside.
equipment.system_note: Some jobs are easier outside than dragging dusty parts through the airlock. The crew fix rover parts and equipment here, in their suits.

equipment.label: Tall Light Post
equipment.description: A tall grid-powered light for paths and work areas.
equipment.system_note: Mars nights are long and very dark. Fixed lights mark the way between the airlock and work areas, but they draw on the habitat's power.

equipment.label: Path Beacon
equipment.description: A small solar route marker.
equipment.system_note: Beacons mark safe routes, so someone returning in the dark or a dust storm can find the airlock.

equipment.label: Portable Floodlight
equipment.description: A battery floodlight for outdoor worksites.
equipment.system_note: A battery floodlight can be carried to wherever work is happening, without running cables from the habitat.

equipment.label: Safety Barrier
equipment.description: A freestanding barrier for marking hazards.
equipment.system_note: Barriers mark hazards such as a drill site, unstable ground or a rover working area, so nobody walks into danger.

equipment.label: Solar Floodlight
equipment.description: A floodlight with its own solar panel and battery.
equipment.system_note: Its own solar panel charges a battery by day, so it shines at night without drawing on the habitat's power.

equipment.label: Hazard Bollard
equipment.description: A bright marker post with a warning light.
equipment.system_note: Bright posts mark the edges of routes and work areas. Their lights blink so they can be seen through dust.

equipment.label: Compact Reactor
equipment.description: Visual model of the site's compact reactor.
equipment.system_note: A compact reactor makes steady power day and night, and through dust storms that cover solar panels. Its radiators shed waste heat into the cold.

equipment.label: Ice Extractor
equipment.description: Visual model of the site's ice extractor.
equipment.system_note: Mars has water frozen underground. The drill heats the ice, pumps up the water and stores it in the tank for the habitat.

equipment.label: Oxygen Generator
equipment.description: Splits water into oxygen using electricity (electrolysis).
equipment.system_note: Makes the oxygen the crew breathe by splitting water into oxygen and hydrogen with electricity, like the oxygen generator on the International Space Station. The oxygen goes into the cabin air; the hydrogen is vented outside. It needs a steady supply of water and power.

equipment.label: Crew Lander
equipment.description: The lander that brought the crew to Mars.
equipment.system_note: The spacecraft that brought you down to the surface: a small pressurised cabin on landing legs. It's always a safe place to shelter and save, but it's far too small to live in for long. That's why you need a habitat.

equipment.label: Galley Table Set
equipment.description: A table for four with chairs: somewhere to sit down and eat together.
equipment.system_note: Shared meals are one of the biggest boosts to crew morale on long missions, and a table gives the day a rhythm.

equipment.label: Galley Oven
equipment.description: A compact convection oven with an induction hob on top.
equipment.system_note: Heats food without open flames. In a sealed habitat, fire and smoke are serious dangers, so cooking is electric and carefully ventilated.

equipment.label: Rehydration Station
equipment.description: Hot and cold water for freeze-dried food pouches.
equipment.system_note: Most food arrives freeze-dried, which makes it light to launch. Adding hot water brings it back to life, using some of the base's water.

equipment.label: Galley Freezer
equipment.description: A fridge over a freezer, for fresh crops and frozen meals.
equipment.system_note: Keeps fresh food from Hydroponics and frozen meals safe. It runs all day and night, so it's a steady load on the power system.

equipment.label: Plastics Hopper
equipment.description: A hopper for sorted plastics, ready to be shredded and reused.
equipment.system_note: Plastic waste can be shredded and melted into filament for the 3D printer: rubbish becomes spare parts.

equipment.label: Metals Hopper
equipment.description: A hopper for scrap metal: cans, offcuts and broken parts.
equipment.system_note: Every kilogram launched from Earth is precious, so scrap metal is kept for repairs instead of thrown away.

equipment.label: Compost Hopper
equipment.description: A hopper for food scraps and plant waste, turned into compost.
equipment.system_note: Organic waste breaks down into nutrients for the grow trays, closing the loop between the galley and Hydroponics.

equipment.label: IV Drip Stand
equipment.description: A wheeled pole with fluid bags and an infusion pump.
equipment.system_note: Gives fluids and medicine straight into a vein, for dehydration, illness or injury, when the nearest hospital is months away.

equipment.label: Crew Vitals Monitor
equipment.description: A wall screen showing every crew member's heart rate, oxygen level and temperature.
equipment.system_note: Wearable sensors send each person's vital signs here, so problems are spotted early, and doctors on Earth can see them too.

equipment.label: Surgery Cart
equipment.description: A wheeled cart with drawers of instruments and a sterile tray.
equipment.system_note: Keeps sterile instruments together and ready. On Mars the crew must be able to handle emergencies themselves.

equipment.label: Exam Light
equipment.description: A bright examination lamp on a wheeled stand.
equipment.system_note: Bright, shadow-free light for examining injuries and doing small procedures.

equipment.label: Work Desk
equipment.description: A desk with drawers, a laptop and a mug.
equipment.system_note: Crew spend hours on reports, experiments and messages home. A personal desk helps with focus and routine.

equipment.label: Crew Chair
equipment.description: A swivel chair on castors.
equipment.system_note: Light and adjustable. In Mars gravity (about a third of Earth's), chairs can be built much lighter.

equipment.label: Open Shelving
equipment.description: Open shelves with storage tubs on the bottom shelf. The other shelves are free for kits, crates and odds and ends.
equipment.system_note: Labelled tubs mean anyone can find tools and spares fast: important when something breaks.

equipment.label: Potted Plant
equipment.description: A potted plant: a little green in a world of red.
equipment.system_note: Studies on the ISS and in Antarctic bases show that looking after plants improves crew wellbeing.

equipment.label: Whiteboard
equipment.description: A wall whiteboard for plans, sketches and the day's schedule.
equipment.system_note: Quick to update and needs no power: perfect for the day's tasks, sketches and reminders.

equipment.label: Regolith Printer
equipment.description: A gantry 3D printer that builds wall panels, shelving and crates from Martian soil. Needs a regolith intake outside.
equipment.system_note: Every kilogram launched from Earth is expensive. This printer binds Martian soil (regolith) into building material, so walls, shelves and crates can be made here instead of shipped. NASA has tested 3D-printed habitats for exactly this reason.

equipment.label: Regolith Intake
equipment.description: Visual model of the site's regolith intake.
equipment.system_note: A scoop wheel digs Martian soil, a sieve drum grades it, and a conveyor feeds it underground to the regolith printer.

equipment.label: Crew Mug
equipment.description: A mug with the mission band. Coffee optional.
equipment.system_note: On the ISS crews drink from pouches with straws. In Mars gravity, about 38% of Earth's, an ordinary cup works again.

equipment.label: Crew Tablet
equipment.description: A tablet on a folding stand, loaded with checklists and procedures.
equipment.system_note: ISS crews follow step-by-step procedures on tablets, so nothing is done from memory.

equipment.label: Laptop
equipment.description: An open laptop for planning, email home and data logging.
equipment.system_note: The ISS runs on dozens of laptops. On Mars, a message to Earth takes 4 to 24 minutes each way.

equipment.label: Paper Books
equipment.description: Three paper books. Heavy to ship, but nobody wants to read only screens.
equipment.system_note: Each astronaut's personal kit allowance is about 1.5 kg, and books are a popular choice.

equipment.label: Photo Frame
equipment.description: A photo of Earth taken from Mars: a small blue star in the night sky.
equipment.system_note: In 2014 the Curiosity rover photographed Earth from Mars: a bright point of light, like a star.

equipment.label: Chess Set
equipment.description: A magnetic chess set, mid-game. The pieces can be printed.
equipment.system_note: In 1970 the Soyuz 9 crew played chess against ground control by radio. Pieces this simple can be printed from Mars-made material.

equipment.label: Zero-G Plush
equipment.description: A plush bear in a little suit, the crew's mascot.
equipment.system_note: Crews carry a small plush toy as a zero-g indicator: when it starts to float, the rocket has reached orbit.

equipment.label: Herb Pot
equipment.description: A small pot of basil for the galley.
equipment.system_note: ISS crews have grown lettuce, kale and chilli peppers. Fresh greens add vitamins and lift morale.

equipment.label: Desk Lamp
equipment.description: An LED lamp on a jointed arm.
equipment.system_note: The ISS uses LED lights that change colour through the day to help crews sleep on a schedule.

equipment.label: Water Bottle
equipment.description: A refillable water bottle.
equipment.system_note: The ISS recovers about 98% of its water, including from sweat and urine. On Mars every litre is recycled too.

equipment.label: Sample Jars
equipment.description: Three sealed jars of regolith in a carry tray.
equipment.system_note: The Perseverance rover seals rock cores in tubes, ready for a future mission to bring them back to Earth.

equipment.label: Toolbox
equipment.description: A sealed toolbox with latches.
equipment.system_note: Mars dust is fine and sticky and gets into everything, so tools are kept in sealed boxes.

equipment.label: Ration Packs
equipment.description: A stack of food pouches.
equipment.system_note: Space food is freeze-dried or heat-treated. For Mars, NASA wants food that stays good for five years.

equipment.label: Guitar
equipment.description: A guitar on a floor stand.
equipment.system_note: A guitar has been on the ISS since 2001. In 2013 Chris Hadfield recorded Space Oddity there.
